title: IPv6 Prefix Options for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) version 6
summary: Defines DHCPv6 options for delegating IPv6 prefixes automatically. A delegating router, typically an ISP's, hands a long-lived prefix to a requesting router across an administrative boundary, without needing to know the topology of the links where the prefix will be used. It has been replaced by RFC 8415.

plainLanguage.summary: An ISP gives your home router a whole block of addresses, like handing you a street of house numbers, and your router hands them out inside. RFC 8415 has since replaced this.

questions: how does an isp delegate an ipv6 prefix
what are dhcpv6 option codes 25 and 26
subtitle: How an ISP's router hands a whole IPv6 prefix to a customer's router using DHCPv6 options.

tldr.problem: A service provider needs an automatic way to give a customer's router a block of IPv6 addresses to divide among its links, without knowing the customer's network layout.
tldr.mechanism: Two new DHCPv6 options, IA_PD and IA_PD Prefix, let a requesting router ask for prefixes and a delegating router hand them out with lifetimes, using the normal DHCPv6 message exchanges.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3633 has been obsoleted by RFC 8415 and updated by RFC 6603 and RFC 7550, so current implementations follow those documents.

facts.label: Recommended T1 and T2
facts.value: .5 and .8 times the shortest preferred lifetime

today: RFC 3633 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8415, so new work should follow that document. It was also updated by RFC 6603 and RFC 7550.

sections.title: Delegating Prefixes with DHCP
sections.content:
RFC 3633 adds DHCP options for the delegation of IPv6 prefixes. A delegating router acts as a DHCP server. A requesting router acts as a DHCP client and asks for prefixes to be assigned. The mechanism suits cases where the delegating router knows nothing about the networks behind the requesting router and needs only the requester's identity to pick a prefix.

The typical example is a service provider assigning a prefix to customer premises equipment (CPE) acting as a router between the subscriber's network and the provider's core. Prefixes are expected to be long-lived, because many applications expect stable addresses. During renumbering the old and new prefix are expected to co-exist for a time.

The document must be read together with the DHCPv6 specification, RFC 3315. This use of DHCP is separate from assigning addresses to hosts, and the RFC notes that no mechanism exists to pass delegated prefixes to a DHCP server serving hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Your internet company owns a huge block of numbers. This memo is the polite way for your router to ask for a piece of it and get a piece back.

sections.title: Model and Example Network
sections.content:
The delegating router is given IPv6 prefixes to hand out. The requesting router asks, the delegating router chooses and replies, and then the requesting router is responsible for what it received. It might, for example, assign a subnet to one of its interfaces and begin sending router advertisements for it.

In the RFC's example, an aggregation device in the ISP network is the delegating router and the CPE is the requesting router. In a typical scenario the CPE subnets a single delegated /48 prefix into /64 prefixes and gives one to each link in the subscriber network. The requesting router may also learn DNS and NTP server addresses from the ISP and pass them on to hosts through its own DHCP server.

Each prefix has a valid and a preferred lifetime, which together are an agreement about how long the requesting router may use it. The requester can ask for an extension and MUST stop using a prefix when its valid lifetime expires.
sections.plainLanguage: The big router at the internet company gives your home router a large block. Your home router cuts it into smaller blocks, one for each part of your house, and returns it when the loan ends.

sections.title: Identity Associations for Prefix Delegation
sections.content:
An IA_PD (Identity Association for Prefix Delegation) groups and manages a set of related prefixes. It is the prefix equivalent of the IA used for addresses in RFC 3315. Unlike an IA, it does not have to be tied to exactly one interface: one IA_PD may cover the whole router, a set of interfaces or a single interface. A requesting router must create at least one IA_PD.

The IAID identifies the IA_PD, is chosen by the requesting router and must be unique among that router's IA_PDs. It MUST stay the same across restarts, either by storing it in non-volatile storage or by an algorithm that gives the same value while the configuration is unchanged. A router using only one IAID can use a well-known value such as zero.

An IA_PD has no lifetime of its own. It is considered expired when the valid lifetimes of all its prefixes have expired. The times T1 and T2 tell the requester when to contact the delegating router, or any available one, to extend lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: An IA_PD is a labelled folder that holds the blocks your router borrowed. The label stays the same even if the router is switched off and on.

sections.title: The IA_PD and IA_PD Prefix Options
sections.content:
The IA_PD option (option code 25) carries the IAID, T1, T2 and an IA_PD-options field. Its option-length is 12 plus the length of the IA_PD-options field. The prefixes live in IA_PD Prefix options placed in that field, and a Status Code option there reports the result of any operation. A message may hold several IA_PD options.

The IA_PD Prefix option (option code 26, called OPTION_IAPREFIX) carries a preferred lifetime, a valid lifetime, a prefix length in bits and a 16-octet IPv6 prefix, plus optional IAprefix-options. Its option-length is 25 plus the length of those options. A lifetime of 0xFFFFFFFF means infinity.

A requesting router may send zero for T1, T2 or the lifetimes to say it has no preference. It may also set the prefix to zero with a prefix-length to hint at the size it wants. The delegating router recommends T1 and T2 at .5 and .8 times the shortest preferred lifetime. A requester discards any prefix whose preferred lifetime exceeds its valid lifetime, and discards an IA_PD whose T1 is greater than T2 when both are above zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The first option is the folder with its label and reminder times. The second is a single note inside it saying which block you got and how long you can keep it.

sections.title: Message Exchanges and Behavior
sections.content:
Prefix delegation reuses the standard DHCPv6 exchanges. The requesting router sends a Solicit containing an IA_PD option, and delegating routers answer with Advertise. It then sends a Request and receives a Reply carrying the prefixes. Before the valid lifetime ends it sends a Renew (or Rebind) and gets updated lifetimes back. A Release returns a prefix. Confirm and Decline are not used.

How the delegating router picks prefixes is left open. The RFC lists static assignment tied to an ISP subscription, dynamic assignment from a pool, and selection by an external authority such as a RADIUS server. If it has no prefixes to give, it advertises an IA_PD with the status code NoPrefixAvail, and the requester MUST ignore that Advertise.

After a valid Reply, the requesting router subnets each delegated prefix onto its downstream links. It MUST NOT assign a delegated prefix or subnet to the link on which it received the DHCP message. Messages SHOULD go out the upstream interface. If a delegating router finds a prefix missing from a requester's binding, it returns it with lifetimes of 0. A Reconfigure message from the delegating router prompts the requester to send its prefixes again.
sections.plainLanguage: Your router calls out for help, a big router offers a block, and your router accepts it. Before the loan runs out, your router asks to keep it a bit longer.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
A rogue delegating router can issue bogus prefixes, which may cause denial of service through unreachability. A malicious requesting router may exhaust the delegating router's available prefixes with repeated requests. Both sides SHOULD use DHCP authentication as described in RFC 3315. On point-to-point links where a man in the middle is not a concern, or where layer two authentication is trusted, DHCP authentication or IPsec may not be needed. Networks that use delegated prefixes should avoid inappropriate advertisement of them.

IANA assigned option codes 25 (OPTION_IA_PD) and 26 (OPTION_IAPREFIX) and status code 6 for NoPrefixAvail.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake helper could give your router a wrong block, and a greedy router could ask for so many blocks that none are left. Checking who is talking to you stops both.

messages.label: Solicit (IA_PD)
messages.note: Asks for delegating routers that can give prefixes.

messages.label: Request (IA_PD)
messages.note: Asks to fill the IA_PD with prefixes.

messages.label: Renew
messages.note: Sent before the valid lifetime expires.

messages.label: Reply
messages.note: Returns the prefix with updated lifetimes.

fields.name: option-length
fields.desc: 12 plus the length of the IA_PD-options field.

fields.name: IAID
fields.desc: Unique identifier of this IA_PD, 4 octets.

fields.name: T1
fields.desc: Seconds until the requester should contact the original delegating router to extend lifetimes.

fields.name: T2
fields.desc: Seconds until the requester should contact any available delegating router.
